Leadership to pursue ‘full and rigorous party self-governance’ with ‘not the slightest hesitation or retreat’, Xi says as fifth plenum ends
Chinese President Xi Jinping has mounted a direct defence of the campaign for strong Communist Party governance and internal discipline, describing them as a “fundamental guarantee” for China’s rise and warning against any easing of scrutiny, according to state media.
Xi took the floor as the party’s 20th Central Committee closed its fifth plenum on Thursday, to directly address the scepticism over the sweeping campaign, state news agency Xinhua reported on Sunday.
According to “side notes” released by Xinhua on a document formally approved at the end of the four-day plenary session, Xi emphasised the need to “further raise awareness of the importance and urgency of relentlessly advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”.

articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: Avelo Airlines CEO reveals the habit he credits for his success
articles.content_orig:
Avelo Airlines founder and CEO Andrew Levy shares how hard work, vulnerability and personal accountability have shaped his approach to leadership.
Andrew Levy has spent three decades in the airline industry, building a career that has taken him from airline startups to the executive ranks of one of the nation's biggest carriers .
Through it all, the Avelo Airlines founder and CEO says that hard work has remained a constant throughout his career.
"Working really, really hard. That's the truth," Levy told FOX Business.
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A FAMILY TURNED CRAFT BEER INTO A HOLIDAY TRADITION
Levy began his aviation career at ValuJet Airlines and later became a co-founder of Allegiant Air, where he held several leadership roles, including president. He went on to serve as chief financial officer of United Airlines before launching Avelo in 2021.
The Avelo CEO also pointed to authenticity and a willingness to show vulnerability as lessons that have shaped his leadership.
CEO SUNDAY: ATOMIC WINGS CEO SHARES HIS JOURNEY FROM WALL STREET TO THE RESTAURANT BUSINESS
Avelo Airlines founder and CEO Andrew Levy says hard work is the habit that has had the biggest impact on his success. (Avelo Airlines)
"I think there's two things," Levy said. "I think one is always be genuine to yourself. And the second one is don't be afraid to show vulnerability."
Levy said vulnerability can sometimes be viewed as a "weakness" in leadership, but he sees it differently.
"The best career advice I think I've received is to just not be afraid to be vulnerable and to show your vulnerability," he said.
Asked about one task he refuses to delegate, Levy said he prefers to handle tough conversations himself.
"Giving bad news," he said. "I think that in my role especially, that it's really important to deliver the good, the bad and the ugly, but not hide behind somebody else to do that, but do it myself."
Levy also pushed back on the perception that being a CEO is an "easy" job.
"It's anything but," he said. "It's constant work. It's a constant focus, attention. It consumes your life."
CEO SUNDAY: DENNY’S CEO SHARES THE SIMPLE RULE GUIDING HIS TURNAROUND OF THE ICONIC DINER CHAIN
Before launching Avelo in 2021, Levy was a co-founder and president of Allegiant Air and later served as chief financial officer of United Airlines. (Avelo Airlines)
He said people may see the title and compensation that can come with running a company without recognizing "the challenges and the toll it takes on you and the investment you have to make as a person to actually be in that role."
"I think there's an underappreciation for how hard it is and the responsibilities that you carry in that role," he added.
For those looking to enter the airline industry, Levy said being comfortable with uncertainty and constant change is essential.
"It's dynamic, it's exciting, but it's constant change," he said. "And you have to enjoy that. You have to enjoy some level of chaos."
If he were not running an airline, Levy said he could see himself working at an investment firm or in private equity, where he could learn about different businesses and industries.
"I would be interested in that only because I get to just see lots of different things," he said, pointing to his "itch" for "constantly learning."
Long before reaching the C-suite, Levy said his first jobs involved raking leaves, pulling weeds and mowing lawns — "whatever I could do to make a little bit of money as a kid."
Asked a series of rapid-fire questions, Levy offered a glimpse into his preferences and personality.

He described himself as a "night owl" who does "a lot of work at night" and said he prefers working in the office.
Asked for his least favorite corporate buzzword, Levy pointed to "laser focused."
"It makes no sense," he said, with a laugh.
When asked for one word his team would use to describe him, Levy answered: "Intense."

articles.title_orig: Gen Z protests turn violent in Germany
articles.title_zh: Gen Z protests turn violent in Germany
articles.content_orig:
Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent on Saturday evening with police using water cannons to disperse crowds and masked rioters smashed shop windows, as officials warn the day of rallies organized by a youth-led movement was infiltrated by extremist factions.
Saturday’s action across Germany, organized by the ‘Gen Z has got this!’ movement, railed against the high cost of living, underfunding in education, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service . It follows a wave of similar protests which have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which saw a third straight weekend of rallies.
Despite organizers calling for the protests to remain peaceful, violence broke out in some German cities, most notably in Frankfurt and Cologne. Police used water cannons while masked protesters smashed shop windows.
Speaking to German tabloid Bild, Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt said that “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities” hijacked the peaceful protests, without elaborating further.
The interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Frankfurt, warned that “around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists” infiltrated the city’s protest as the evening descended into violence and looting.
“It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended,” Roman Poseck said.
Poseck said he was determined the violence that has rocked France would not be replicated in Germany.
“We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” he said, according to Reuters. “France must not be held up as a model in this regard.”
In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows were smashed. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop. According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, several people broke into shops in downtown Frankfurt and over 30 people had been temporarily detained in city by the late evening.
Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. “Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals – not against peaceful participants,” the police said in a statement.
In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers were attacked. “There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) … our riot police are taking immediate action against this,” the police said.
Berlin police wrote on X that 27 officers in the German capital had sustained minor injuries and just under 60 people had been detained for offenses including property damage, assault, and resistance against emergency forces.
The movement’s organizers have sought to distance themselves from the ensuing violence. “We had no influence on what happened after the demonstrations ended,” a spokesperson from their press team was quoted by Der Spiegel as saying.
Organizers of ‘Gen Z has got this!’ planned the day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. According to the organization, 120,000 people attended the protests across Germany on Saturday.
“We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us,” the movement states on its website.
Speaking for his reasons for joining the movement, an 18-year-old student protester in Munich told Reuters, “The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us.” In the eastern city of Dresden, demonstrators held placards reading, “The rich want war, the youth want a future!” and “You’ve screwed up – Gen Z will sort it out.”
More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement took place in France on Saturday, in what was billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24.
This time, however, they were more scaled down than before. The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris; a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week.
The French protests were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that “radical elements at the tail end of the processions” in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, “attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting.”
Protests over soaring housing costs also swept Portugal and Italy on Saturday. In the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, thousands marched to demand Portugal’s center-right government withdraw a rental bill they say will worsen the country’s housing crisis.
In Italy, protests largely led by student groups and workers rallied against inflation, stagnant wages and unaffordable housing in cities including Turin, Bologna and Milan.
CNN’s Pierre P Bairin contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now
articles.title_zh: AI stocks just lost $5 trillion — but history says the stock market's sweetest stretch starts now
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
The AI trade just had its scariest October in years. The rest of the stock market barely noticed.
The biggest AI and chip stocks have shed about $5 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Alphabet ( GOOGL ) have each given up roughly $835 billion in market cap, and Intel ( INTC ) lost nearly half its value in October.
Everything else? The other 625 large US stocks in that tally added about $1.3 trillion. And while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) slipped this week, 9 of its 11 sectors rose about 1% or more, something that hadn't happened in any week since at least 1999, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
Jeff Hirsch, editor of the Stock Trader's Almanac , has a name for this: "Octoberphobia." And he's buying the sell-off.
"I did buy some today... this is an opportunity here," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Friday . "The damage isn't as bad as the headlines are."
Hirsch also has the calendar on his side. October selloffs like this one often lead into what the Almanac calls the sweet spot of the presidential election cycle , which runs from the fourth quarter of a midterm year through the following June.
From the last October close of a midterm year to the end of the following June, the S&P 500 has risen 19 times out of 19 since 1950 , with a median gain of about 15%. Chip stocks have been 8-for-8 since 1994, with a median gain of about 22%.
The ride wasn't always smooth. Chips fell another 11% or so before turning higher in 2002 and 2018, and eight cycles is a relatively small sample.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) tumbled about 17% in October, yet it's still up more than 50% this year.
On Friday, it dipped as low as $460, below the $464 low from July 29 that marked this summer's bottom. Then it closed at $472, back above that line. That's the look of a bear trap — a breakdown that reverses, catching traders betting on more losses.
Hirsch likes the timing. "Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," he said. His firm placed a new buy in the sector on Friday.
Bulls first need to reclaim about $524, the top of last week's bounce, then the early-October high near $596. Losing the July low would put the February-April range near $370 in play. That's about 21% below Friday's close.
Not everyone is loading up the shopping cart.
BofA's Michael Hartnett said it's "risk-off until global rate hike ends," pointing to 42 central bank rate hikes worldwide over the past six months. The Fed held on Wednesday , but two officials voted to hike. Hartnett's line in the sand for chips is $520 on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF ( SMH ), which closed Friday near $522. On SOXX, that works out to about $469, just above the July low it barely held.
So the bulls' and bears' lines sit almost on top of each other. Hirsch said he'd change his view on a decisive break of the S&P 500's mid-September low near 7,550, less than 1% below Friday's close.
Tuesday's midterm vote comes first. Then November, the S&P 500's best month of the year , gets its turn.

articles.title_orig: Binance resumes withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies after $6 billion heist
articles.title_zh: Binance resumes withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies after $6 billion heist
articles.content_orig:
Binance said Sunday it had resumed withdrawals for some major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereal after more than $6 billion in assets were stolen from the cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance is the world's largest crypto exchange by daily trading volumes. News of the hacking attack, which is thought to be the biggest-ever crypto heist, caused the prices of most major cryptocurrencies to fall sharply on Friday.
However, the company has offered reassurances it would cover 90% of the losses from the attack using company funds to buy tokens to replenish a large portion of what was stolen.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the attack but said they would be resumed in phases, the first of which began on Sunday.
"First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals," the exchange posted on X .
As of 5 a.m. Eastern Time, Binance said it had restored withdrawals for Bitcoin, Ethereal, BNB, XRP, Base, Doge and Optimism, and that it would "continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed."
The FBI accused North Korea of being behind the hack in a statement on Saturday, confirming earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a Pyongyang-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was responsible.
TraderTraitor is the same group blamed for a $1.5 billion theft from the Bybit platform in February last year.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," the statement said.
The FBI added that it had observed "TraderTraitor actors" converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralized finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."

articles.title_orig: Binance to Resume Customer Withdrawals in Phases After Hack
articles.title_zh: Binance to Resume Customer Withdrawals in Phases After Hack
articles.content_orig:
Which topics should we dive deeper into?
Select what genuinely interests you. Your picks feed directly into our editorial planning.
Crypto news that's actually worth your time.
Weekly. 60 seconds. Carefully curated by our editors: no hype, no promo flood, no spam.
Here is what is confirmed: Binance opened the first withdrawal phase after the October 29 attack on Sunday morning, and the Dogecoin network is one of the 15 networks in that phase. The reserve snapshot dated October 31 lists ten balances as fully backed, and Dogecoin is not one of them. Our assessment follows further down: for DOGE holders the reopened withdrawal route weighs more than the missing backing line, because the way out of the exchange is what makes a decision possible at all.
The price itself has barely moved. Dogecoin traded at $0.0758 on Sunday morning, up 1.20 percent over 24 hours on CoinGecko data, as of November 1 at 9.41am CET. Market capitalisation stands at $11.86bn, which ranks DOGE 12th. Bitcoin trades at $78,060 over the same period and is up 1.07 percent, so the market is exhaling evenly without any single coin standing out.
Three days after the largest theft a crypto exchange has suffered, withdrawals are running again. In a notice dated November 1 at 4.08am UTC, Binance announced the first phase for Sunday between 6.00am and 9.00am UTC. The release does not come all at once but network by network: each pairing of asset and network passes its own security and readiness tests before it opens. Deposits worked normally throughout, the exchange says. How the timetable came about and what was promised beforehand is set out in our overview of the first withdrawal phase .
The 15 networks in the first phase are, as reported by crypto.news , the Bitcoin network, Ethereum, the BNB Smart Chain, Tron, Solana, the XRP Ledger, Zcash, Dogecoin, Polygon, the Avalanche C-Chain, Arbitrum, Base, Optimism, TON and Sui. Binance ordered them by last week's demand. A network on the list, however, does not mean every route inside it opened at the same minute.
By late Sunday morning in Europe, the exchange's network status showed bitcoin over the Bitcoin network, ether over Ethereum, and USDT, USDC and BNB over Ethereum and the BNB Smart Chain as withdrawable again. Further networks from the first phase follow step by step. To see where a DOGE route stands, check the withdrawal dialogue on the exchange itself rather than a press release.
This is the line that goes under in most reports. Alongside the reopening, Binance is filling the hole from its own funds. By the evening of October 30 about 80 percent of the stolen amount had been replaced, according to the exchange, 90 percent on October 31 and 95 percent on November 1. The stolen sum stands at roughly $6.3bn, and TRM Labs analysis traces it to the North Korean group TraderTraitor.
The October 31 reserve snapshot shows ten balances as fully backed: bitcoin, ether, USDT, BNB, Solana, USDC, XRP, USD1, RLUSD and Zcash. Dogecoin is not among them. The remaining five percent of the affected assets consist, on the same account, of less liquid tokens outside those ten. DOGE therefore falls into the group for which no explicit backing pledge exists so far, even though the coin ranks 12th by market capitalisation.
That sounds sharper than it is meant, and it is still a difference. An absent mention is no proof of a hole. The omission only means that Binance has not yet produced a figure for this balance that a customer could point to. For bitcoin or XRP such a figure exists. For DOGE it does not.
A proof of reserves is an exchange's evidence that on a fixed date it holds at least as many coins as its customers have deposited with it. It has two halves: the documented holdings on the exchange's addresses, and the sum of customer balances those holdings are measured against. Only together do the two say anything, and even then only for the cut-off date.
Binance has announced the full proof, with a zero-knowledge attestation, for Tuesday, November 3. Until then the October 31 snapshot is the only reading available. What such a report can show and what it structurally cannot is broken down in our piece on the announced proof of reserves . For DOGE holders that means the figure against which a pledge could be recalculated arrives on Tuesday at the earliest.
The path from an exchange outage to the price rarely runs through panic selling. It runs through turnover. Someone who cannot withdraw trades more cautiously, because every position sits for the time being inside a system nobody is leaving. Market makers in that situation quote smaller sizes at wider spreads, since they can no longer hedge their risk freely between venues. The order book thins out, and a thin order book moves further on the same order size.
That effect was measurable on Saturday. Our piece on the thinnest trading day of the month showed that by Saturday evening Dogecoin worth $0.77m changed hands on Kraken across 2,582 trades, against $3.96m and 7,986 trades in the October average. The price stood at $0.0758 then, and the $0.0750 level held.
Since then nothing much has changed in the price, but the setting has. Dogecoin trades today at the same $0.0758, the $0.0750 level is still holding, and 24-hour volume across all tracked venues stands at $265m. The open withdrawal route is the new element. Whether it brings turnover back can only be read off the days after the release, not off the announcement itself.
The daily range runs from $0.074962 to $0.076166, a span of 1.61 percent between low and high. Narrow, though a little wider than Saturday. The lower boundary is the more interesting one: the low of the past 30 days sits at $0.075137 and dates from October 30, the day after the attack. The current price is just 0.9 percent above it.
On the upside the nearest reasoned level is the daily high at $0.076166, and above that the area around $0.0790, where Dogecoin found a footing several times between October 18 and October 23. On the downside the monthly low comes first. If it breaks, there is no zone with meaningful trading over the past 30 days until the area around $0.0695.
To place the monthly balance: Dogecoin stood at $0.094506 on October 1 and at $0.07588 on October 31. Across the month that works out at a loss of 19.7 percent. October counts as a traditionally strong month in crypto; in 2026 it was DOGE's weakest since the spring.
A look across twelve months places the situation better than any daily range. On November 1, 2025 a DOGE cost $0.1864 and market capitalisation stood at $28.25bn. Today the figures are $0.0758 and $11.86bn. The price has lost 59 percent in a year, the market capitalisation 58 percent.
Bitcoin is down 29 percent over the same stretch. Dogecoin has therefore given up roughly twice as much as the benchmark, which fits the usual pattern: coins with smaller capitalisation and more sentiment-driven demand swing harder in both directions. Supply does not explain the decline. Circulation stands at 156.54 billion DOGE and grows through the fixed issuance by about five billion units a year, so by a good three percent. The rest is demand.
The past three days have demonstrated the difference between the two forms of custody in practice. Holding DOGE on an exchange means owning a claim against that company, not a coin. In normal times the claim is as good as a coin, and in an outage it is exactly as mobile as the exchange lets it be. Holding the coins in your own wallet means owning the private key and being able to send at any time, whatever state an exchange is in.
Set against that is an honest price. Self-custody shifts the risk from the company to your own diligence: a lost seed phrase is final, and so is a wrongly confirmed transfer. articles.title_orig: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu’s Bid to Stay in Power Will Test His Political Savvy
articles.content_orig:
President Isaac Herzog on Sunday called on Israel's political leaders to accept the election results and demonstrate flexibility in coalition negotiations, warning against political entrenchment that could force the country into another election, ahead of consultations at the President’s Residence set to begin on Wednesday.
“The election results are an established fact – they are the reality. And now is the time to tell all the leaders: Stop climbing trees and position yourselves in front of this reality," Herzog said while speaking at the state memorial ceremony for Israel's first president, Chaim Weizmann.
Herzog made the remarks amid the political deadlock in which the election results showed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanayhu's bloc and the bloc seeking to oust the premier both fall short of the required 61-seat Knesset majority.
Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead, securing 53 seats in the next Knesset, while the opposition bloc won 48. Meanwhile, the Arab parties, Ra'am and the Joint List, won a record-breaking total of 19 seats combined.
The Joint List and Ra'am are expected to recommend Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot for prime minister during consultations with President Isaac Herzog, a senior Joint List official told Walla on Sunday.
Talks at the President's Residence will begin Wednesday, when Eisenkot is expected to be the first candidate to receive the mandate from the president, giving him 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension, to form a coalition.
Along with the 48 seats won by the opposition bloc, the Arab parties' 19 recommendations would give Eisenkot 67 in total, prompting Herzog to grant him the mandate.
The Knesset is expected to be sworn in on November 10, regardless of any government or coalition talks.
By law, the president is required to consult the Knesset factions before deciding who receives the task of forming a government.
Herzog said that this week, at the President’s Residence, "we will try to put up ladders to allow the leaders to position themselves in front of this reality in a measured and careful manner."
Herzog said he would receive the official election results on Wednesday from Central Elections Committee chairman and Supreme Court Deputy President Justice Noam Sohlberg.
"Following that, I will begin consultations at the President's Residence. The President's Residence will be wide open to all factions and parties."
The president emphasized the importance of cooperation among party leaders, urging them to demonstrate a willingness to consider different proposals and reach agreements.
"I have already said that I hope the representatives will come with open minds, and I add that they should come with open hearts, to listen and share ideas and find creative solutions to prevent another election ," he said.
On Saturday, Eisenkot laid out four principles for joining his proposed coalition, saying that “any MK” willing to accept them could become a partner in forming the next government.
Eisenkot said he intended to establish the broadest possible Zionist, statesmanlike government, bringing together elected representatives who agree on Israel’s fundamental character, national service obligations, and the need to eliminate Hamas’s military and governing capabilities in the Gaza Strip.
Last week, Democrats party leader Yair Golan called on Wednesday for the opposition to form a coalition with the Arab parties.
Other heads of the opposition parties, Eisenkot, Naftali Bennett (B'Yachad), and Avigdor Liberman (Yisrael Beytenu), had drawn a red line to Arab parties being part of the government, saying they are not viable coalition partners after the October 7 massacre in 2023.
The political deadlock could ultimately lead to another election, although the parties may still reach an agreement through coalition negotiations. Other possible outcomes include a unity government among Netanyahu and members of Eisenkot’s bloc, or the formation of a minority government.
The Arab parties have expressed willingness to cooperate with the oppostion bloc to work toward replacing Netanyahu.
Meanwhile, opposition party leaders have also reportedly agreed that their first move after the new Knesset is sworn in on November 10 would be to oust Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana , a member of Netanyahu's Likud party.
The move would require a majority in a Knesset vote and could be achievable with the support of the Arab parties, bringing the potential backing to 67 seats.
Replacing Ohana would give the opposition bloc greater control over the parliamentary agenda, including votes, legislation, and committee appointments, even if Netanyahu remains in office as head of a caretaker government.
Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Jeff Deehan is a real estate developer by day and a "hobby guy" by night.
The 42-year-old has a workshop in his East Lansing house. One project remained elusive: a small piece of steel to secure a camper to his truck. While Deehan was toying with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra in voice mode, he described the piece he needed and the angle at which it would sit. Five minutes later, the chatbot had prototyped it.
Deehan told GPT-6 that he knew of a company called SendCutSend that does custom sheet-metal fabrication. The chatbot downloaded its design as a DXF file, opened SendCutSend's website, filled in the form, and paid the $156 with the payment information he'd stored. Ten days later, it was on his doorstep.
"In about 10 minutes, I spoke a part out of my mind into existence, without touching my phone," he said.
Deehan is part of a growing class of enthusiasts who are building physical gizmos with AI's help. They use chatbots to build prototypes, then send the AI-generated files to manufacturers, boutique fabricators, and their home 3D printers .
Modeling physical items with AI has its risks. Deehan was sure his prototype would be a millimeter off here or there, though it ended up being right on. Other vibe manufacturers said that their products took multiple iterations, burning through their budgets.
Normies have long used AI to write software, now dubbed " vibe coding ." These builders say AI is coming for hardware creation, too — and they're calling it "vibe manufacturing."
Amy Zhou and Jake Fitzgerald are building an open-source tool for vibe manufacturing. They call it "text-to-CAD" — and it already tops 23,000 stars on GitHub.
Zhou previously worked on the iPhone cases team at Apple and is now a design engineer at the AI rendering startup Vizcom. Fitzgerald wanted to get back into robotics after pivoting to crypto. They text new ideas back and forth between San Francisco and New York.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
The duo hopes to upend CAD, or computer-aided design . CAD engineers use software to design and optimize 3D models. It takes training and skill. The vibe manufacturers say you can do it easily with a large language model.
Zhou makes jewelry with AI. The 25-year-old's previous startup turned pictures users uploaded into 3D models of charms, then cast the models in wax. It made a necklace for Cluely's CEO , Roy Lee, before Zhou left the business. She still occasionally makes AI-rendered charms for friends when they want necklaces of their pets.
Fitzgerald is more interested in making robot arms. Using the text-to-CAD tool, the 31-year-old designed the arm in sheet metal and paid about $200 to have it built by SendCutSend. It has 0.6 meters of reach, with a motor and a camera, and he considers it an "edutainment" product to learn about robotics before the industry booms .
A few months ago, Fitzgerald saw "compounding failures" when the AI would build bad designs on top of bad designs. The screw holes came in loose, for example. He spent about $2,000 repeatedly ordering pieces. With GPT-6 Astra, he said that's no longer a problem.
Sourish Sharma has watched AI change CAD. The 20-year-old from London got an MRI scan for a research study three years ago and asked for his data. He got a 3D printer and used an open-source tool to turn the data file into something printable. The tool didn't work very well, so he had to edit it by hand. "Some of the folds of the brain were not very foldy," he said.
Now, Sharma has a much bigger printer — and AI. With one prompt, GPT-6 Astra blew the open-source tool out of the water, converting the data and making what he considers a more accurate brain. He's printed out a life-size one, as well as a handful of miniatures that he gives to friends.
"AI literally does replace CAD engineering completely," Sharma said. "It's kind of unfortunate if you're a CAD engineer. Fortunately, I'm not."
The more complex a product is, the more difficult it is to vibe manufacture. You won't be able to make a car at home with ChatGPT anytime soon.
There's one population whose products are often simple and accessible: kids. Arthur Prince, a 34-year-old IT worker from outside Paris, said the children's toy he modeled in a week with AI would've taken him months with his CAD knowledge alone.
Prince's toy creates stories and images with AI based on a kid's voice prompt. He developed everything, from the casing to the internal wiring, with GPT-6 Astra, then asked Claude to criticize its work. Once the two chatbots reached a consensus, he ordered 10 of the toys from the Chinese manufacturer JLCPCB for about 500 euros, fretting that he'd wasted his money on something that wouldn't work.
Luckily, they did. Prince's first tester, his daughter, loves it. "She's very proud to see that I can make something like this," he said.
The benefit of vibe manufacturing kids' toys is their simplicity. Many parents don't want their children surfing the web , so AI prototypers don't have to worry about those pesky questions of cell service and web browsers.
David Plakon wanted his kids to leave messages for their grandparents in Florida — but didn't want them on the internet.
The 39-year-old from Austin is a longtime "tinkerer." He's had a 3D printer since 2015, and was printing his kid a " KPop Demon Hunters " sword while we spoke. So, he and his wife, Lara, figured they could build their own answering machine in the style of the Tin Can phone .
Plakon gave GPT-6 Astra some design inspiration and instructions to build a prototype. All of the parts had to be purchasable or buildable with his 3D printer, he told the chatbot. It easily put together a model, instructing him to buy a potentiometer, a speaker, and an ESP32 chip, and guided him through the assembly.
He's now printed the design some 15 times, improving it on each go. Initially, some of the pieces didn't fit together. "AI's good but not perfect," he said.
But the box does work, and he hopes to sell it one day. He's keeping it small-scale for now, aiming to get the answering box in the grandparents' home for Christmas.
"I don't have any delusion that I could send this to a factory, and they would be able to make it," Plakon said. "For now, it's very fun to prototype."

articles.title_orig: How one family gave a critical boost to gene therapy research
articles.title_zh: How one family gave a critical boost to gene therapy research
articles.content_orig:
Glenn (from left), Beckham, Cara and Eliza O'Neill pose for a family photo in 2015. Eliza has Sanfilippo syndrome, a rare inherited disease. Robert Clark hide caption
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
When Eliza O'Neill was little, she was one of those kids who always needed to have an accessory, like a hat or a scarf.
"She would always go get my high heels from the closet and clop around in those — which she scared us to death," says her mom, Cara O'Neill, a pediatrician in Columbia, S.C.
But by the time Eliza turned 3, her parents noticed she was falling behind on developmental milestones. She was diagnosed with a pragmatic speech delay, meaning she had learned a lot of words, for example, but she wasn't using them in a typical way in social situations.
In 2013, one of Cara's colleagues suggested testing Eliza for a group of metabolic disorders — just to rule them out.
But the test came back positive for something called Sanfilippo syndrome .
Cara remembered learning about the rare inherited disease back in medical school.
"When they said the word, it all kind of came rushing back," she says. "And it was just this bale of dread, like, oh, my goodness, this is horrific."
Children with Sanfilippo have a faulty gene that leaves them unable to break down heparin sulfate, a molecule critical to normal cell function. As it builds up in the body, it causes severe complications.
Kids with Sanfilippo lose their ability to speak and walk. They have seizures, and they usually don't live past their teens, according to the Cure Sanfilippo Foundation , which the O'Neills started and continue to run.
For Eliza's dad, Glenn O'Neill, it took a little while after learning Eliza's test results for the diagnosis to sink in.
"It wasn't really until I got home that I realized how quickly the degeneration happened," he says. "And that was really the point where we said, 'Gosh. Whatever we need to do, we need to do it now.'"
At Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio, researcher Haiyan Fu had been working on a gene therapy in mice for Sanfilippo since the late-1990s.
The therapy used a modified virus to deliver a working copy of the broken gene to patients' cells.
Eliza O'Neill gets a kiss from her dad, Glenn, before becoming the first person to receive an experimental gene therapy for her rare disease in 2016. O'Neill family hide caption
Fu realized the experimental therapy was promising. "And if we treat early, it could be potentially a cure," she says. "So I can't give up."
Keeping it going – and funded – was challenging, though. She thought she would have to quit in 2009. But the families of kids with Sanfilippo stopped her.
"They said, 'You can't leave. Can we give you some of the funds for you to, you know, carry on?'" Fu recalls, explaining that these families had helped her from the beginning and didn't want to see her work stop.
In all, eight patient foundations, including Ben's Dream and a Cure for Kirby , kept Fu's work going until the research was ready for the first human trial.
But a clinical trial would be expensive. Glenn O'Neill had an idea for how to raise the money.
"We reached out on a whim to some strangers that we found on the internet about making a viral video," he says, referring to filmmaker Benjamin Von Wong, who made them a video over a few days in 2014.
In the spring of 2014, the Saving Eliza video helped the O'Neills break GoFundMe's record at the time, raising a million dollars in just a few weeks. Soon, it hit $2 million.
The money raised helped fund the first human trial, which started in May 2016.
The experiments were promising enough for the biotech industry to take notice.
Ultimately, a biotech company called Ultragenyx acquired the rights to the gene therapy in 2022 and kept studying it. A few years later, the company submitted data to the Food and Drug Administration for review.
The FDA approved the gene therapy in September. The one-time infusion is called Fayuvi.
"The treatment will work best the younger the child is because the more brain is remaining," says Ultragenyx CEO Emil Kakkis. "By the time they're 2 or 3 or 4 years old diagnosed, getting figured out, they've lost a lot of ground. And we have treated a few kids that were in the 6-month age that have done really well. And our view is that when you treat them really young, you actually get better gene therapy results."
Ultragenyx set the price for the treatment at nearly $4 million, tying it for the second most expensive gene therapy ever, according to 46brooklyn , a drug price research firm.
Kakkis says Ultragenyx is committed to making sure every patient is treated, regardless of the price. "There should be no logistical location, site or state or other kind of rule that stops us from getting the patient treated. We understand what [we've] got to do."
Moments after the FDA approval was announced, Fu got a call from Cara O'Neill — and messages from other families that funded her research. Some had lost a child along the way.
Fu says Fayuvi's approval is good news, but it brings mixed emotions for her: "It shouldn't take this long."
As for Eliza, she's almost 17 now. She was the very first patient to get the gene therapy as part of a clinical trial back in 2016.
Because she was 6 years old when she was treated with the gene therapy, she had already lost her ability to speak. It never returned, but she can communicate with picture cards and devices. Eliza goes to school. And this summer, she swam and learned to float on a pool noodle.
"I just feel proud of my girl. You know?" Glenn O'Neill says. "I feel proud of her. It's been a rough road for her, but we also know she's very lucky."

articles.title_orig: A third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
articles.title_zh: A third weekend of protests in France as youth-led rallies sweep Europe
articles.content_orig:
Akhtar is a foreign correspondent for The Telegraph based in London
French protesters donned Hallowe’en costumes and threw Molotov cocktails at police officers as street demonstrations turned violent in Europe for a third consecutive weekend.
Clowns, witches and pirates marched alongside a Spider-Man, a Frankenstein’s monster and a zombie Michael Jackson, as several thousand demonstrators moved through eastern Paris under a circling police helicopter.
“No need for tear gas to make our future look bleak,” read one placard. Another read: “Dressed up as an angry citizen for Hallowe’en.”
At the Porte de Charenton, on Paris’s south-eastern edge, a riot squad was holding back protesters when someone hurled a Molotov cocktail into their ranks, setting several officers on fire and forcing the unit to fall back.
Dozens of masked people dressed in black used hammers to pry up paving stones and hurl them at police.
Meanwhile, violence erupted on Saturday night in Berlin and Frankfurt, where masked looters smashed shopfronts and attacked police officers.
Authorities in France, bracing for a repeat of the rioting that erupted two weeks ago, flooded the country with 70,000 security officers and rerouted the Paris march to the outer reaches of the capital.
The interior ministry put the nationwide turnout at around 15,000 by early afternoon, and said the situation remained “generally calm”, with 27 arrests reported by 2pm.
But as night fell in Paris, clouds of smoke and small fires could be seen at several locations, and police fired tear gas to disperse demonstrators.
Nearly half a million people demonstrated across the country, including 200,000 in Paris, according to a coalition of youth organisations and unions representing high-school and university students.
Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, pointed to an “extraordinary” level of violence from some, blaming far-Left extremist groups for attacks on security forces, and said Hallowe’en was not an excuse to break the law.
He described the throwing of a Molotov cocktail at a riot police officer in Paris as an “attempted murder,” adding that the officer had escaped with minor injuries. “We are fully prepared for those looking for confrontation tonight,” he added
Covering one’s face at a protest with intent to disrupt public order remains an offence, punishable by a €150 (£125) fine. Police said that children in costume would not be treated as suspects.
Authorities imposed overnight curfews in the Place de la République and Les Halles districts from 11pm to 6am, and closed more than 40 metro and suburban stations close to government buildings and landmarks.
In preparation for the marches, shopkeepers across the country boarded up their storefronts.
“Behind these boards, there is neither power nor an enemy. Just a family and its work,” read a message scrawled on plywood covering one Paris business.
Police said they arrested more than 290 people across the country on Saturday.
“The marches proceeded smoothly within the framework of the declared demonstrations,” the ministry said, while noting that “radical elements” in several cities, including Bordeaux, Toulouse and Marseille, had attempted to enter city centres “with the aim of carrying out vandalism and looting”.
The unrest is part of a wider wave of youth-led protests sweeping Europe.
In Germany, a movement calling itself “Gen Z regelt” – which translates roughly as “Gen Z’s got this” – rallied in some 34 cities, including Berlin, Frankfurt and Munich, demanding greater investment in education, health and climate protection, and opposing any return of military conscription.
But by Saturday evening some of the protests had turned violent, with masked looters attacking shops in Frankfurt.
Police responded by firing water cannons at young people who were hurling Molotov cocktails. Several police officers were injured and a large section of Frankfurt’s main shopping precinct was shut down.
There were also violent clashes in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
Organisers in Germany said more than 180,000 people had registered online, though only several thousand had turned out by Saturday afternoon. Some people were dressed in Hallowe’en outfits ranging from dinosaurs to Batman.
Roman Poseck, interior minister for the state of Hesse, said that “around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists” had infiltrated the protest in Frankfurt.
“It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended”, he said.
At Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate, students pressed for more spending on schools and housing.
“At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken,” said Janelle Schultz, a high-school student.
In the German capital, a protest not organised by the GenZ regelt movement took place in the evening, with police reporting they were pelted with eggs and bottles.
Similar gatherings or alerts were reported in Italy, Albania, the Netherlands and Spain.
France’s protests began last month with high-school students protesting about dilapidated buildings, teacher shortages, and a university admissions system that is regarded as unfair to poorer students.
It has since drawn in “yellow vest” activists, trade unions, and others angry at Emmanuel Macron, the French president, and has broadened its demands to include the protection of civil liberties and the right to protest, after a security clampdown left some demonstrators seriously injured.
Authorities counted about 550,000 marchers on Oct 17, when looting and arson caught the government off guard, and 410,000 the following Saturday, when police still made more than 1,300 arrests.
Jean-Luc Mélenchon , the hard-Left presidential candidate, who has accused the country’s government of “taking an increasingly authoritarian turn”, joined the march in Paris.
Student unions vowed to blockade schools and universities on Tuesday and Thursday before a union-backed demonstration on Nov 5.
The protests come as the presidential elections are less than six months away and Marine Le Pen, the far-Right leader, is leading the polls.
With the eurozone’s second-largest economy on the brink of recession and under pressure to curb its debt, the French government has little room to placate protesters with new spending.
Mr Macron said this week that it was “not normal” for France to be in such “turmoil” so close to an election.

articles.title_orig: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
articles.title_zh: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
articles.content_orig:
Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday.
The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added.
Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so.
"Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday.
In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack.
It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack.
The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits.
Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury.
All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said.
The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible.
North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks.
Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach".
Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism".
On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners.
The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance.
Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide.
Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers.

articles.title_orig: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
articles.title_zh: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
articles.content_orig:
Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia 's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.
Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."
Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.
On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.
Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."
The List, which emerged from the student revolt , is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote , leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.
Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.
The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control ; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime .
The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died . The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.
Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.
"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."
Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.
It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia , an organization that monitors the work of governments.
The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.
However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.
The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.
"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.
Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.
"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.
Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.
The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump loses allies after elections in Serbia and Brazil
articles.content_orig:
The midterm elections in the United States are just around the corner: On Tuesday, November 3, American voters will choose their representatives to the US Congress. The right-wing-conservative Republican party of President Donald Trump currently has a majority in both chambers.
But in other parts of the world election results are already in. The majority of voters in both Serbia and Brazil cast their ballots for left-wing parties. Those results will not influence the midterms in the US, but the victories of the Student List in Serbia and the incumbent president, Luiz Inacio "Lula" da Silva , in Brazil are bad news for Trump all the same.
In Serbia, he has lost an important European ally in outgoing president Aleksandar Vucic . And in Brazil, the Trump camp had been hoping Flavio Bolsonaro would triumph.
"Trump was a strong supporter of both Jair Bolsonaro , the Trump-like figure who served as president before Lula defeated him in 2022, and of his son Flavio," says Lawrence J. Haas, a senior fellow for US foreign policy at the American Foreign Policy Council, who was communications director for Al Gore, Bill Clinton's vice president, in the 1990s. "Trump wasn't happy about the defeat of either Bolsonaro," he continues, "and he doesn't feel warmly toward Lula. So relations will remain cool at best."
Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation in Brazil for alleged corruption and money laundering. After losing the election, he fled the country for Florida . The US State Department granted him and his family entry visas in spite of the pending legal action.
Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat. Instead, he claims there were irregularities in the vote. This is very reminiscent of Trump, who continues to claim – falsely – that Joe Biden and the Democratic Party "stole" the US election in 2020. Trump's comments on Bolsonaro's defeat sounded very familiar. "It looked like another rigged election, frankly," the US president said on Monday. "Elections have to be indisputable – and it looked very bad to me."

Aleksandar Vucic had ruled Serbia as president with an iron fist since 2017. He resigned just before these elections in order to stand as prime minister, a role he previously held from 2014 to 2017. Vucic has commented in the past that he and President Trump are like-minded people. Trump's eldest son, Donald Jr., visited Vucic in Belgrade shortly before the US presidential elections in November 2024, and again a few months later.
The US Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC), which is closely connected with Trump's MAGA ("Make America Great Again") movement, recently announced that it was organizing a meeting in Belgrade in November, at which Vucic was to be a keynote speaker. It is unclear whether this is still the case.
Another thing Vucic and Trump have in common is that the soon-to-be-ex-president of Serbia has a much more positive attitude toward Russian president Vladimir Putin than do most other European heads of state. Vucic did not join EU countries in imposing sanctions on Russia after it launched its war of aggression against Ukraine . Belgrade still buys Russian raw materials, and Serbian state media under Vucic presented a more positive image of Russia than of the EU.
Trump also seems increasingly inclined toward Moscow. His special envoy Steve Witkoff recently described Putin as a " humanitarian ," while, in an interview, Trump himself openly admitted that he got on better with Putin than with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy . The end of the Vucic government now means that Trump has lost one of his few allies in Europe who takes a similar view.

There's still a chance of an outcome in the Israeli elections that might be to Trump's liking. With more than 96% of votes counted, the right-wing bloc led by prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu is in the lead. However, Trump ally Netanyahu has lost his majority, and the coalition negotiations will be very difficult.
Trump and Netanyahu have been close allies since well before February this year, when they joined forces to launch a war against Iran. In 2018, during his first term in office, Trump moved the US embassy in Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. This was controversial, because both Israel and Palestinians claim Jerusalem as their capital. Netanyahu's camp welcomed the decision.
Today, the United States is still by far Israel's most important partner, while Israel is an important regional ally for the US. It is not clear what their relationship would be like with a different Israeli government. If Netanyahu remains in power , little, if anything, will change.
With Vucic's defeat, Trump has lost a loyal ally. And Lula's victory means, for him, that a disagreeable president remains in power. None of this is good for Trump, but foreign policy analyst Haas said it won't influence the important midterm elections in his country. "Americans will be voting [...] on the basis of issues that affect them, and how they feel about the party in power."
But this doesn't bode well for Trump, either. "Trump has the lowest approval rating of any president on the eve of a mid-term election since Harry Truman in 1946," Haas explained. "Americans are very concerned about issues of affordability, [and] they strongly oppose the US-Iran war."
Benjamin Alvarez Gruber in Miami contributed to this report, which was originally written in German.

articles.title_orig: Why Wendy’s is losing the burger wars—and is now a takeover target for Nelson Peltz
articles.title_zh: Why Wendy’s is losing the burger wars—and is now a takeover target for Nelson Peltz
articles.content_orig:
In the burger wars currently raging in the United States, there is one clear loser among the major chains: Wendy’s. Its fortunes have declined so much that it’s now the target of Nelson Peltz’s Trian Fund Management, which is offering to take the restaurant private for $1.4 billion, a sum that’s not even 1% of McDonald’s market value.
The restaurant chain, once beloved for its “fresh, never frozen” beef and reputation for being a higher-quality fast-food option, has been struggling for 18 months. Its promotions have fallen flat, intense competition has stolen customers, and a revolving door in the corner office has deprived it of the focus needed to get out of its rut. Long the second-largest U.S. burger chain behind McDonald’s, Wendy’s has slipped to third place behind a resurgent Burger King.
In May, Wendy’s overhauled its management, hiring Potbelly’s turnaround veteran Bob Wright as its fourth CEO in three years, as well as Potbelly’s finance chief Steve Cirulis as CFO, in an effort to reassure Wall Street that Wendy’s was in steady hands. For a time, it worked: “Wendy’s turnaround prospects have improved under [Wright and Cirulis] whose successful Potbelly revamp supports a strategy focused on the menu, marketing, operations, and digital capabilities,” Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Michael Halen wrote in a research note.
Despite the confidence in Wendy’s new C-suite, shares remain under pressure and are 65% below where they were three years ago, when sales began to stagnate. (Shares briefly hit a 20-year low in June.) So it’s hardly surprising that Wendy’s is now the target of Peltz’s Trian, which would rather turn the restaurant chain around far from the glare of the public markets.
Wendy’s was founded in 1969 when Dave Thomas, a former Kentucky Fried Chicken franchisee, opened a restaurant and named it for his daughter. It quickly found a niche with its distinctive square hamburger patties, chili, and Frosty desserts that differentiated the chain from McDonald’s. It even had some pop culture moments, most notably in 1984 with its famous “Where’s the Beef?” campaign.
The chain has had many ups and downs over the years, but it started to show cracks in earnest last year, when quarterly sales declined.
In its most recent quarter, U.S. sales at its established restaurants fell 7%, the sixth decline in a row. More worryingly, visits to U.S. stores slumped 12.5%, suggesting many Wendy’s patrons are falling out of the habit of eating there. Wendy’s will report its third-quarter results on Thursday, and they will be heavily scrutinized for any signs of a reprieve. Analysts expect Wendy’s to report a U.S. same-store sales decline of about 6%.
In his first conference call with analysts in August, Wright, a Wendy’s alum who once worked with the chain’s legendary founder Thomas, showed he was clear-eyed about Wendy’s many problems. The list includes a lack of compelling value menu items for budget-conscious diners and inconsistent execution at its restaurants. Wright has told franchisees and investors that Wendy’s had lowered the quality of its ingredients in a quest to save costs and had allowed service to become uneven due to insufficient staffing. New promotions—like its Minions & Monsters kids’ meals—and new menu items—like a new chicken sandwich—have fallen flat. Wendy’s has also tried and failed to find a winning formula for breakfast, long a weak spot for the chain, but angered franchisees in the process by adding operational complexity and costs with little payoff.
High beef costs are pinching profits: net income fell 40% in the first half of 2026.
And Wendy’s carries an enormous debt load of $2.4 billion that’s roughly equivalent to its annual revenue. (Wendy’s systemwide sales in the U.S. were $12 billion last year, but because it operates mostly as a franchise model, its revenues are simply its cut of those sales, plus rent and fees from its franchisees.)
“Our quality differentiation has eroded, our value proposition has weakened, and we have not consistently delivered the experience customers expect from Wendy’s,” said Wright, who was Wendy’s operations chief from 2013 to 2019 before going to Potbelly.
Competitors have jumped at the chance to capture Wendy’s market share.
Burger King’s same-restaurant sales rose 8.5% last quarter as it executed its “Reclaim the Flame” turnaround plan that remodeled half its restaurant fleet and revamped its flagship Whopper hamburger, leading to a 20% jump in sales of the sandwich.
McDonald’s has problems of its own , but they are not as deeply rooted as Wendy’s, and the market leader is still clocking sales growth, however modest.
Shake Shack’s same-store sales rose 3.5% in its most recent quarter.
Given the depth of Wendy’s problems, the company in August withdrew its full-year 2026 financial outlook and cut its dividend dramatically, saying store traffic would remain weak for the rest of the year.
Peltz, whose Trian Fund Management owns 16% of Wendy’s, had long expressed interest in taking the restaurant private. It first did so in 2022 and then again in February before tabling its $1.4 billion offer this week. Trian has held shares in Wendy’s since 2005, and Peltz’s son Brad and former Trian partner Peter May serve on its board.
“Wendy’s sits at a critical juncture,” Peltz wrote in a letter to Wendy’s board on Thursday. “The business requires significant capital investment to de-lever [or reduce debt] and execute the strategic initiatives needed to turn system performance around.”
The prospect of Wendy’s fixing itself without the pressure of Wall Street is appealing to some. “A take-private makes sense as Wendy’s turnaround is likely to be prolonged given the challenged state of the lower-income consumer and soft state of the quick-service burger category,” TD Cowen wrote in a note.
Wendy’s board said it has formed a committee to review Trian’s proposal, and the company itself said it was “acting” with urgency on its turnaround.
But signs that this process could get messy didn’t take long to surface. One investor, Blackwells Capital, accused Peltz of being opportunistic by waiting for Wendy’s shares to sink lower before re-upping his interest in buying the company. The firm also said that given Peltz’s long ties to and influence over Wendy’s, the restaurant chain’s problems—and by extension its stock decline—are “the consequences of his own disastrous tenure.” A Trian spokesperson declined to comment.
A potential take-private process, or any drama around it, is typically distracting for CEOs trying to execute a turnaround. Wright transformed Potbelly in his five years at the helm by sprucing up its menu and offering more deals to attract diners on a budget, all while the company was a frequent target of activist investors. The improvements at Potbelly ultimately led to it being taken private by RaceTrac, a major gas station and convenience store chain. Wright was patient and methodical in fixing Potbelly and is showing signs he is approaching Wendy’s troubles in the same way.
“It’s going to take time,” Wright said in August. “But these issues are within our control.”

Kyiv has repeatedly struck Russian oil and gas sites in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure since Moscow began its offensive there in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: WW2 Cinderella Service crew remembered after 'ultimate sacrifice'
articles.title_zh: WW2 Cinderella Service crew remembered after 'ultimate sacrifice'
articles.content_orig:
Three World War Two veterans who served in the South West and died in the conflict, are among those being added to a memorial.
Sqn Ldr George Crawford and Pilot Officer Kenneth Brian Willson were both based at St Eval RAF base in Cornwall while Sgt Jack Saul Lockwood was based at RAF Chivenor in Devon, as part of Coastal Command.
Coastal Command was tasked with keeping British seas safe from German U-boats along with escorting allied shipping convoys of troops, food and munitions.
It was recently announced 12,500 men and women who died while serving with the Coastal Command, part of the Royal Air Force, would be added to International Bomber Command Centre's Losses Database .
Crawford was a pilot with No. 53 Squadron Coastal Command and flew Consolidated B-24 Liberator aircraft from St Eval.
He flew with a multi-national crew which included people from Canada and New Zealand. He took part in 21 operations and had been tasked with patrolling the English Channel during the D-Day landings.
It was during this mission his plane was hit by anti-aircraft fire from a U-boat, leading to the death of him and the whole crew. Crawford was 29 and the only body found was that of a crew member from New Zealand.
The International Bomber Command Centre said the project was poignant as more than half the people who made the "ultimate sacrifice" had no known grave.
Crawford - who was from Ham, which was then part of Surrey but now in the London Borough of Richmond upon Thames - was given a Distinguished Flying Cross medal in January 1944 for an attack on a U-boat.
"As is the case with more than half of the airmen who were lost in the service of Coastal Command, the remainder of the crew have no known grave, and their names are instead included on the Runnymede Memorial," a spokesperson from International Bomber Command Centre said.
Four months after his death, Crawford's wife Leslie gave birth to a son in Belfast and named him George David Hugh Crawford.
Coastal Command was also known as the 'Cinderella Service' due to how it was overlooked and underfunded as Bomber Command and Fighter Command took priority during the war.
Many of the crews were based in south-west England as they headed out to protect waters off Devon and Cornwall's coast.
Willson served with No. 58 Squadron Coastal Command at RAF St Eval.
The International Bomber Command Centre said Willson, who was born in Dartmouth, Devon, on 11 April 1923, was part of missions including bombing attacks on the port area of German city Bremen and anti-submarine patrols in the Bay of Biscay.
The centre said during the latter, squadron record books said: "P/O Willson had the good fortune to sight two separate U-Boats.
"The first one was attacked and six depth charges dropped on the track on the submarine.
"An oil patch 100 yards in diameter was visible but nothing further seen.
"The second U-boat was attacked by the front guns and bullets seem to strike the conning tower and the U-boat crash-dived; nothing further was seen of this submarine."
Willson was on another anti-submarine patrol on 12 June 1942 when the crew in his aircraft became disorientated in dense fog and crashed near Cabo Ortegal in Galicia on the northern tip of Spain.
All six crew were killed and were buried side-by-side in the Bilbao British Cemetery.
Lockwood grew up in the Lincolnshire village of Scampton , which had its own RAF connections as the location where the Dambusters set off for Operation Chastise .
He trained as a pilot in Canada and the US before being posted to No. 179 Squadron Coastal Command at RAF Chivenor in Devon.
He flew modified Wellington bombers with special headlights known as Leigh Lights, which helped locate submarines just below the surface at night.
On his crew's third operation on 12 and 13 August 1943, Lockwood died as their aircraft returned to Chivenor.
Due to poor visibility, the crew decided to make another circuit to establish their position, but crashed into a nearby hill before the aircraft exploded due to unused depth charges still being on board.
The International Bomber Command Centre said the body of Lockwood, who was 23, was returned to Scampton where he was laid to rest within sight of the family farm he grew up on.
His epitaph reads: "He died that we might live in freedom."

articles.title_orig: Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
articles.title_zh: Rioters smash, loot storefronts amid cost of living protests in Germany
articles.content_orig:
Masked rioters smashed storefronts and looted goods late Saturday in Frankfurt, Germany amid a protest against the rising cost of living.
The largely peaceful demonstrations were led by a youth initiative called "Gen Z regelt" - roughly translated to "Gen Z's got this" - rallied in more than 30 cities "for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life," and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available.
Tensions peaked in the evening as some groups of protesters refused to disperse, sparking clashes and violence in major cities including Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg.
in Frankfurt's financial hub, masked protesters hurled stones, fireworks and pepper bombs, according to police.
Authorities also said looters stole weapons from a gun store, which were later retrieved. Some rioters also threw Molotov cocktails at police after pummeling them with stones and bottles earlier in the day, Frankfurt police said on X.
In the northern city of Hamburg, some protesters also shot pyrotechnics toward police and burned down barricades. Police responded by using water cannons and tear gas to disperse the crowds.
Earlier in the day, demonstrations had been largely peaceful. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.
"We call for more money to be invested in social services and education, as well as in climate protection - in short, in our future - because we are the ones who will be affected by this the longest and who will have to live with it," high school student Lara Breitenbach said.
Janelle Schulz, another high school student from Berlin, also said that the authorities had to invest more money in education.
"At my school, the ceiling is collapsing because of water damage, nothing is being done about it, we have a shortage of teachers, the toilets are broken," she said.
